name: Butter Chicken Pasta

ingredients.buy: 2 lb 5 oz dry short pasta (penne, rigatoni or rotini)

writer_notes: All 20 locked ingredient lines are used by a step; no step introduces an unbought item. Reserved pasta water is water, not a purchased line.
No cost_lines or cost_ps were provided in the dispatch, so cost prose uses the ${{cost_ps}} token and shop_smart deliberately makes no traceable per-package cost arithmetic claim.
Cal and protein rendered as {{cal}} and {{protein}} tokens; locked values are 630 cal and 40.2 g protein per serving.
Cuisine labeled Indian Fusion, not authentic butter chicken, since this is a pasta adaptation.
Scaling verified as source x3.5 across every line (base ~4 servings to 14).

prose.intro_html:
Butter chicken is one of those restaurant orders that feels like a treat and hits your card like one too. This is the version that lives in your fridge instead. We take the same warm, creamy, lightly spiced tomato sauce that makes butter chicken worth craving, and we build it around chicken breast and a pot of short pasta so it stretches across fourteen dinners without asking you to stand at a stove every night.

Here is the honest pitch. It comes in at {{cal}} calories and {{protein}} grams of protein a serving, it tastes like you tried a lot harder than you did, and the whole thing is one pan of sauce plus one pot of pasta. If you have ever wanted takeout comfort on a meal-prep budget, this is the recipe that quietly does both.
prose.shop_smart:
The spice rack is where this dish either saves you money or robs you, so let's shop it right.

  • Garam masala, cumin, coriander, chili powder and turmeric are the whole personality of the sauce, and you use them by the teaspoon. Buy them from the bulk bins or the value-size jars rather than the little branded shakers, because you are pulling a few teaspoons from a jar that will season a dozen more batches.
  • Tomato sauce (passata) is the body of the sauce and you need a good amount of it, so buy the larger bottles or cans instead of grabbing several small ones. Fewer packages, less packaging you are paying for.
  • Chicken breast is the protein you are building the whole plan on, so buy the large family pack and portion it yourself at home. The small trays cost more for the same meat.
  • Almond butter and half and half are the two things that make this taste rich. A jar of almond butter goes a long, long way when you only spoon in a few tablespoons, and it keeps for months, so one jar carries this dish and plenty of breakfasts after it.
  • Short pasta means penne, rigatoni or rotini. Any of the three grabs the sauce well, so buy whichever shape is cheapest on the shelf that week.
prose.make_it:
This is a one-pot sauce and one-pot pasta job. Get the pasta water going and the pan hot, and you are most of the way there.

  1. Cook the short pasta to al dente, following the package directions. Before you drain it, dip out a cup or two of the starchy pasta water and set it aside. That water is your thinning tool later, so do not skip it.
  2. In a large pan over medium heat, warm the olive oil and butter together. Add the chicken pieces and cook until they are golden on all sides.
  3. Stir in the diced onion, the garlic and the ginger. Keep it moving for two to three minutes, until everything softens and smells sweet.
  4. Add the garam masala, cumin, coriander, chili powder, turmeric and red chili flakes. Cook for one minute, stirring constantly, so the spices bloom in the fat instead of scorching.
  5. Stir in the tomato paste and the tomato sauce (passata) until it all comes together. If it looks too thick, loosen it with a splash of that reserved pasta water.
  6. Stir in the almond butter, then pour in the half and half. Bring it up to a boil, then drop the heat and let it simmer four to five minutes until the sauce thickens.
  7. Add the cooked pasta to the pan and toss until every piece is coated in the sauce.
  8. Stir in the chopped cilantro, season with salt and black pepper to taste, and it is ready to portion.
prose.portion_html:
Here is the trick that keeps fourteen containers honest. Do not eyeball it. Set your empty pan on the scale and note the weight, then weigh the pan again once it is full of finished pasta and sauce. Subtract the empty weight, and that is how much cooked food you actually have.

Divide that number by fourteen, and now you know the target weight for each container. Scoop to that weight, container by container, and every single one carries the same {{cal}} calories and {{protein}} grams of protein. No short portions on Thursday because Monday got greedy. Top each one with a little extra cilantro if you saved some, snap the lids, and you have two weeks of lunches or dinners that all pull the same weight.
prose.cost_closing_html:
So what does butter chicken comfort cost when you make it fourteen at a time? It lands at ${{cost_ps}} a serving.

Put that next to a single butter chicken takeout order, which will run you the better part of fifteen dollars once you add the rice, and the math stops being close. You are getting the same craving satisfied, plus {{protein}} grams of protein to actually keep you full, for a fraction of one restaurant plate.

That is the whole idea here. Eating well is not about spending less on worse food, it is about spending a little effort up front so good food costs you almost nothing per plate. Fourteen dinners, one afternoon, one honest price.
